teaching.task: # Maths S11 N01: What is a network, and where do networks appear in real life? Vertices for objects and edges for connections, the same network in any drawing, real systems as networks, the questions networks answer, and drawing one from a description (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: A network is a collection of objects joined by connections. Each object is drawn as a dot, called a vertex. More than one are called vertices. Each connection is drawn as a line between two vertices, called an edge. In the flight network, each city is a vertex, and each route is an edge. Count them. Seven vertices and ten edges. An edge always joins exactly two vertices, and it only says those two are connected. How long a line is drawn doesn't matter at all. You can fly straight from Perth to Sydney, so there's an edge. You can't fly straight from Hobart to Darwin in this network, so there's no edge. But you can still get there by changing planes, moving from vertex to vertex along the edges. Hobart to Melbourne, Melbourne to Adelaide, Adelaide to Darwin. Here's the surprise. Watch the dots move. Perth slides to the right, Hobart floats to the top, and the lines stretch and bend to follow. It looks completely different, but every city is still joined to exactly the same cities as before. So it's the same network. A network only records what's connected to what. Distances, compass directions and the shapes of roads are left out, unless we write them on. That's why a network diagram usually isn't drawn to scale. That's exactly what a train map does. It squashes and straightens the real tracks, because a passenger only needs to know which stations connect, and in what order. Two drawings show the same network whenever they have the same vertices joined by the same edges, even if the lines cross. Once you start looking, networks are everywhere. Mobile phone towers pass signals to each other. Each tower is a vertex, and each link between two towers is an edge. A rail trail for bikes has junctions and paths. The junctions are vertices, and the paths between them are edges. A town's water pipes join the reservoir, the pumping stations and the streets. A delivery van has a list of stops, and the roads between stops are the edges. A school's classrooms and corridors, the stops on a bus route, even the links between web pages, it's the same idea. Even a social media app is a network. Each account is a vertex, and each connection between two accounts is an edge. The trick is always the same question. What are the objects, and what joins them? Answer that, and you can draw the network.

# Maths S11 N01: What is a network, and where do networks appear in real life? Vertices for objects and edges for connections, the same network in any drawing, real systems as networks, the questions networks answer, and drawing one from a description (design)

Status: Revision 3 (25 Nov 2026): preflight and fact repairs (see the final section, "Revision 3 (root, 25 November 2026)"). Revision 1 (24 Nov 2026): first design, written to the maths visual standard (`../maths-visual-standard.md`), `math-s11-t01.md` to `t06.md` (Revision 1, this batch), the Year 12 designs that recall this strand (`math-s12-c01a.md`, `c02.md`, `c03.md`, `f01.md`), the coherence audit and root's Standard rulings 1 to 99. Not voiced. Next: student learning review and Codex maths check, then voicing on the Google voice and a build on the studio kit to grade A.

Narration 5,508 characters by script (see "Narration length estimate"), 13 scene headings, about 495 s with holds (key notes fixed at 45 s). Nothing recorded; human listening pending.

Scope: first video of the Year 11 Networks, paths and trees strand, outline playlist order 54. One video for Standard 1 and Standard 2. Viewers arrive from t06's final frame. Pre-design pack: `../pre-design/maths-standard/math-s11-n01.md`. Route entry: `math-s11-n01` in `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-13.json`. Site lesson: `year11/networks-paths-and-trees/lesson01.sa.html` (card 05 and its "position doesn't matter" insight; degree and directions are n02's). Visual system: maths studio kit; the phone tower, rail trail and delivery van plates (all existing); the networks and maps coded.

Owner rules applied: header strip "NETWORKS, PATHS AND TREES" only; one question; one stage at a time; plain meanings; two attempts with "Pause here to answer." and 10 s countdowns; brief feedback with one crossed slip; five key notes with a framed card; everyday anchors (flights, a train map, phone towers, a rail trail, a delivery run, a social app shown as account dots); no people; Australian spelling; no em dashes.

Syllabus content points (Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 11, Networks, paths and trees, "Network concepts", common to Standard 1 and Standard 2), quoted from `../../programme/maths-standard-route-inputs-13.json`:

- `ci4513c403`: "Describe a network as a collection of objects (vertices) interconnected by lines (edges) that can represent systems in the real world"
- `ci2d693812`: "Examine circumstances in which networks are used in a variety of real-world applications"

Source: https://curriculum.nsw.edu.au/learning-areas/mathematics/mathematics-standard-11-12-2024/content/year-11/fabf235394

**Boundary:** starts from t06's final frame exactly (a coded outline of Australia, about 1,200 px wide, with seven labelled city dots, Perth, Darwin, Adelaide, Melbourne, Hobart, Sydney, Brisbane (blue), joined by ten straight amber example routes; grey strand chip "Time and location: done"; chips "dots and lines", "Next: networks" and "?"). This confirms the t06 to n01 join: t06's provisional mark can be lifted. Teaches: a network, vertices and edges; counting them; travelling along edges; the same network in different drawings; real systems as networks; the questions networks answer; drawing a network from a description. Not taught: degree, directions and weights (n02); tables and maps (n03); paths and trees (n04).

## Decisions

- **Anchor: the flight map with the clocks taken away (t06's frame).** Seven cities, ten routes; what is left is "what's joined to what".
- **Vertices and edges, words first.** "Objects drawn as dots" and "connections drawn as lines", then the names vertex (plural vertices) and edge. Travel goes vertex to vertex along edges (Hobart to Darwin in three flights).
- **The surprise: the same network in a different drawing (recurring model: the network morph).** The dots slide and the edges bend, while a side list of connections stays fixed; a train-map diagram beside a wiggly real track shows why networks drop shape and distance (site card 05's insight).
- **Real systems (point 1) and circumstances (point 2) are different scenes.** Scene 4 asks "what are the objects, and what joins them?" for five systems; scene 5 shows what networks are used to decide: connectivity when a link fails, the best-connected place, the shortest route, the cheapest way to link everything. Each later video answers one (n02 degree, n06 shortest path, n05 minimum spanning tree).
- **Drawing from a description (site card 05).** Vertices first, then edges ticked off one by one.
- **Simulations (standard item 3).**
  1. **Network morph** (scene 3, feedback 2): dots slide to new positions with edges following; a connection list "A: B, C, D ..." stays lit and unchanged; a "same network" check ticks.
  2. **Edge failure** (scene 5): an edge fades (storm icon); a path search lights a route around it; a counter "still connected: yes".
  3. **Edge-by-edge draw** (scene 6, feedback 1): edges draw in turn as a list ticks.
- **Colour roles (fixed n01 to n07).** Vertices blue; edges amber; a highlighted route or tree green-teal (teal); removed or failed edges violet; answer green; mistake red. (n02 adds direction arrows amber and weights in white on amber tags.)
- **Large type, handwritten voice.** Labels 40 px; working 52 px; nothing below 26 px; all text above y = 950. Hand tags: "dots: vertices", "lines: edges", "same connections, same network", "what are the objects? what joins them?", "still connected", "vertices first". At most two live at once.
- **Stage changes (standard item 2).** The flight map (1); the counted network (2); the morph and the train map (3); the real-world gallery (4); the four questions (5); the drawing board (6); framed card (7); question cards (8 to 11); the delivery van's street network (12); key notes (13).
- **Worked examples (g01 order).** Scene 2: "7 vertices, 10 edges" (framed green); "Hobart → Melbourne → Adelaide → Darwin". Scene 5: "Sydney → Adelaide → Darwin → Brisbane: still connected" (framed green). Scene 6: "A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, C-E, D-E: 5 vertices, 6 edges" (framed green).
- **Memory aid.** Framed card: "Dots for things, lines for links." Key line: "A network only records what's joined to what: not distances, not shapes, not where the dots sit."
- **Plain meanings at first use.** Network ("a collection of objects joined by connections"); vertex ("an object, drawn as a dot"); edge ("a connection between two vertices, drawn as a line").
- **Attempts.** A1 (pack question 1): 4 vertices, 5 edges; crossed "4 edges" (caption "count the lines, not the dots"). A2 (pack question 2): the same network; crossed "different: the lines cross" (caption "same connections, same network").
- **Mistake scene:** none separate. Shape matters (3, A2); counting dots for edges (A1); an edge for every pair (6, said); no edge means unreachable (2).
- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) a network keeps only which objects are joined, so a dot and a line are enough (1, 2); (2) moving dots doesn't change what's joined, so many drawings show one network (3); (3) any system of things and links fits this picture once you name the objects and the links (4); (4) with that picture we can ask whether everything stays connected, which place is best connected, the shortest route and the cheapest way to connect all (5); (5) drawing vertices first stops edges being missed (6).
- **Entry knowledge (route):** none beyond Stage 5 (t06's frame).
- **Site notes.** lesson01 recalculated: no error. MSY-28 (point 2 only as a list).
- **Handoff (to math-s11-n02, degree, direction and weight).** Scene 12: board clear; the delivery van `ma12-delivery-van-v1.png` (about 520 px wide) at the left; at the right a coded street network (about 1,000 px wide) of five labelled stops, "Depot", "Bakery", "Café", "Pharmacy", "Gym" (blue dots), joined by amber edges with arrowheads on the one-way streets and minute tags "4", "3", "5", "2", "6", "7", "4" (as n02 scene 4); chips "one-way? how long?", "Next: degree, direction and weight" and "?". n02 opens on this frame.
- **Legacy logic ported:** none.
- **Author notes (not learner copy):**
  (a) Flight network edges (example routes, no airline): Perth-Adelaide, Perth-Melbourne, Perth-Sydney, Darwin-Adelaide, Darwin-Brisbane, Adelaide-Melbourne, Adelaide-Sydney, Melbourne-Sydney, Melbourne-Hobart, Sydney-Brisbane. 7 vertices, 10 edges. Connections each (n02's degrees): Perth 3, Darwin 2, Adelaide 4, Melbourne 4, Hobart 1, Sydney 4, Brisbane 2.
  (b) Without Sydney-Brisbane: Sydney-Adelaide-Darwin-Brisbane (3 flights).
  (c) Rail trail: 5 vertices, 6 edges. A1: 4 vertices, 5 edges; Q and R join three each.
  (d) A2 drawings: (1) square A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left, with edges A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A and diagonal A-C; (2) A top left, C top right, B bottom right, D bottom left, with the same five edges, so A-B and C-D cross. Connections: A: B, C, D; B: A, C; C: A, B, D; D: A, C.

Main question: *A flight map with the clocks taken away is just dots and lines. What is a network, and where do networks appear in real life?*
Entry knowledge: none beyond Stage 5.
Stops after: vertices, edges, the same network in any drawing, real systems, the questions networks answer, drawing from a description.
Handoff: math-s11-n02: "Next: degree, direction and weight".

## Script and shots

Cue words in **bold** trigger the visual change. Colour roles (fixed): vertices blue; edges amber; highlighted routes teal; removed edges violet; answer green; mistake red. Header strip "NETWORKS, PATHS AND TREES". Scene headings in the hand font, 44 px.

On "drawn as a dot" one dot enlarges with tag "vertex" (hand tag "dots: vertices"); on "vertices" all dots tag "vertices". On "called an edge" one line thickens with tag "edge" (hand tag "lines: edges"). scenes.teachingReason: Here's Australia's flight map from last time, with the clocks taken away. Seven cities, and ten routes joining them. Notice what's left. It doesn't matter how far apart the cities sit on the page, or which way the lines point. What matters is which cities are joined. That's the idea behind a network, one of the most useful pictures in maths. Airlines, map apps and phone companies all work with pictures like this. So what is a network, and where do networks show up in real life?

scenes.teachingReason: A network is a collection of objects joined by connections. Each object is drawn as a dot, called a vertex. More than one are called vertices. Each connection is drawn as a line between two vertices, called an edge. In the flight network, each city is a vertex, and each route is an edge. Count them. Seven vertices and ten edges. An edge always joins exactly two vertices, and it only says those two are connected. How long a line is drawn doesn't matter at all. You can fly straight from Perth to Sydney, so there's an edge. You can't fly straight from Hobart to Darwin in this network, so there's no edge. But you can still get there by changing planes, moving from vertex to vertex along the edges. Hobart to Melbourne, Melbourne to Adelaide, Adelaide to Darwin.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the surprise. Watch the dots move. Perth slides to the right, Hobart floats to the top, and the lines stretch and bend to follow. It looks completely different, but every city is still joined to exactly the same cities as before. So it's the same network. A network only records what's connected to what. Distances, compass directions and the shapes of roads are left out, unless we write them on. That's why a network diagram usually isn't drawn to scale. That's exactly what a train map does. It squashes and straightens the real tracks, because a passenger only needs to know which stations connect, and in what order. Two drawings show the same network whenever they have the same vertices joined by the same edges, even if the lines cross.

scenes.teachingReason: Once you start looking, networks are everywhere. Mobile phone towers pass signals to each other. Each tower is a vertex, and each link between two towers is an edge. A rail trail for bikes has junctions and paths. The junctions are vertices, and the paths between them are edges. A town's water pipes join the reservoir, the pumping stations and the streets. A delivery van has a list of stops, and the roads between stops are the edges. A school's classrooms and corridors, the stops on a bus route, even the links between web pages, it's the same idea. Even a social media app is a network. Each account is a vertex, and each connection between two accounts is an edge. The trick is always the same question. What are the objects, and what joins them? Answer that, and you can draw the network.

scenes.teachingReason: So why bother drawing them? Because a network turns a messy real situation into a picture we can reason about. Here are four questions networks help answer. First, is everything still connected if one link fails? Say storms close the Sydney to Brisbane route. Take that edge away. Can you still get from Sydney to Brisbane? Yes, by going Sydney, Adelaide, Darwin, Brisbane. Engineers ask exactly this about power lines and phone links, so that one failure doesn't cut a whole town off. Second, which place is best connected? Adelaide, Melbourne and Sydney each join four others, so they make good hubs. Third, what's the shortest or quickest route between two places? And fourth, what's the cheapest way to link every place, like laying fibre to every tower? We'll answer each of those in this strand, one at a time.

scenes.teachingReason: Let's draw one from words. A rail trail has five junctions, A, B, C, D and E. Paths join A and B, A and C, B and D, C and D, C and E, and D and E. Always start with the vertices. Draw five dots and label them. Then add the edges one at a time, ticking each one off as you go. A to B, A to C, B to D, C to D, C to E, D to E. That's five vertices and six edges. Count again at the end. Six paths in the description, six lines on the page, so nothing's missing. Where you put the dots is up to you. Spread them out, so the lines don't cross more than they need to.
